content: Benazepril, marketed under the brand name Lotensin®, is an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor approved by the FDA for the treatment of hypertension. It is important to note that the information provided here is not intended as medical advice or treatment, and WikiDoc does not endorse any medication or off-label drug use. Black Box Warning Benazepril carries a Black Box Warning due to its potential risks. Common adverse reactions include cough, dizziness, fatigue, and headache. Adult Indications and Dosage Initial Dose (without diuretic use): 10 mg orally once daily. Initial Dose (with concurrent diuretic use): Discontinue the diuretic 2-3 days before starting Benazepril to reduce the risk of hypotension. If blood pressure is not controlled with Benazepril alone, the diuretic can be resumed, and Benazepril should be started at 5 mg orally once daily. Maintenance Dose: 20–40 mg orally once daily or 10–20 mg orally twice daily, with a maximum dose of 80 mg/day. Divided dosing is more effective in controlling pre-dosing (trough) blood pressure than a single daily dose. Dosage Adjustments: Adjustments should be based on peak (2–6 hours post-dosing) and trough responses. If a once-daily regimen does not provide adequate trough response, consider increasing the dose or switching to divided administration. Concomitant Use with Potassium-Sparing Agents: Co-administration with potassium supplements, potassium salt substitutes, or potassium-sparing diuretics may increase serum potassium levels. Monitor potassium levels periodically. Pediatric Use Benazepril is not recommended for children under 6 years of age or for pediatric patients with a glomerular filtration rate (GFR) <30 mL/min due to insufficient data. For children over 6 years, the recommended dose is 0.2 mg/kg orally once daily. For those unable to swallow tablets, a suspension can be prepared following specific instructions. Contraindications Hypersensitivity to Benazepril or any other ACE inhibitor. History of angioedema, whether or not associated with previous ACE inhibitor treatment. Warnings Angioedema: Angioedema involving the face, extremities, lips, tongue, glottis, or larynx has been reported. Laryngeal edema can be fatal. Discontinue Benazepril immediately if angioedema occurs and provide appropriate treatment. Intestinal Angioedema: Patients may present with abdominal pain, nausea, or vomiting. Symptoms resolve after discontinuation of the ACE inhibitor. Anaphylactoid Reactions: Life-threatening reactions have been reported during desensitization therapy with hymenoptera venom and during dialysis with high-flux membranes. Temporarily discontinue ACE inhibitors in such cases. Symptomatic Hypotension: This is more likely in patients who are volumeor salt-depleted due to diuretics, dietary restrictions, dialysis, diarrhea, or vomiting. Correct volume or salt depletion before initiating therapy. Pregnancy: Drugs acting on the renin-angiotensin system during the second and third trimesters can cause fetal toxicity, including reduced renal function, oligohydramnios, lung hypoplasia, skeletal deformities, and neonatal complications such as anuria and death. Discontinue Benazepril as soon as pregnancy is detected. Adverse Reactions Clinical Trials: Adverse events were generally mild and transient, with no significant differences in incidence between Benazepril and placebo groups. Common side effects include cough, dizziness, and fatigue. Rare Reactions: Stevens-Johnson syndrome, pemphigus, photosensitivity, pancreatitis, thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, and eosinophilic pneumonitis have been reported. Laboratory Findings: Rare decreases in hemoglobin and elevations in uric acid, blood glucose, serum bilirubin, and liver enzymes have been observed. Drug Interactions Diuretics: Patients on diuretics may experience excessive blood pressure reduction. Minimize this risk by discontinuing the diuretic or increasing salt intake before starting Benazepril. Potassium Supplements and Diuretics: Concomitant use may lead to hyperkalemia. Monitor potassium levels periodically. Lithium: Increased serum lithium levels and toxicity have been reported. Monitor lithium levels when used with Benazepril. NSAIDs: Co-administration with NSAIDs may reduce the antihypertensive effect of Benazepril and impair renal function, especially in elderly or volume-depleted patients. Monitor renal function periodically. Use in Specific Populations Pregnancy: Discontinue Benazepril immediately upon detection of pregnancy due to fetal risks. Nursing Mothers: Minimal amounts of Benazepril and its active metabolite, benazeprilat, are excreted in breast milk. Use caution. Geriatric Use: Elderly patients are more likely to have reduced renal function. Monitor renal function and adjust the dose accordingly. Renal Impairment: Monitor renal function during the first few weeks of therapy, especially in patients with renal artery stenosis or pre-existing renal impairment. Administration and Monitoring Oral Suspension Preparation: For patients unable to swallow tablets, a suspension can be prepared using Ora-Plus® and Ora-Sweet® vehicles. Store the suspension in a refrigerator and use within 30 days. Monitoring: Regularly monitor blood pressure, renal function, and serum potassium levels, especially in high-risk populations. Overdose Management Monitor blood pressure and clinical symptoms closely. Provide supportive care to maintain hydration and systemic blood pressure.
